What the Author Wrote, What the Agent Reads:
Silent Cue Loss in Enterprise Document Ingestion

Yikai Zhao Affiliation: Amazon Email: yikai@amazon.com    Saurabh Pandey Affiliation: Amazon Email: saurabpd@amazon.com    Pradeep Kumar Misra Affiliation: Amazon Email: pkmisra@amazon.com
Abstract

Enterprise agents act on documents. Before an agent can follow a policy, answer a compliance question or file a ticket, some ingestion layer must turn a Word file or PDF into tokens—and that layer is where an agent deployed in the wild silently loses information. Mature converters recover text, tables and structure faithfully, so the pipeline looks healthy. We show that one layer is lost by all of them—the meaning an author encodes in how text looks—and that the loss makes agents confidently wrong rather than visibly incomplete, which is the harder failure to detect in deployment.

We build a task from 76 real policy documents: recover the requirements the author singled out for attention, scored against the file’s own OOXML properties by a deterministic matcher with no LLM judge. Formatting-blind ingestion collapses from micro F1 0.6900.690 to 0.1500.150 (docling) and 0.0750.075 (plain text), a gap that replicates across six answering models from two vendors—five Claude models spanning the Opus, Sonnet and Haiku tiers, and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6. The failure is silent in a way that matters for autonomy: an agent that cannot see the cue guesses, and docling’s false-positive rate on requirements the author did not flag is four times ours.

A span-level leave-one-out localises the loss to two cues—highlight (+0.302+0.302) and colour (+0.262+0.262), both pHolm<10−4p_{\text{Holm}}<10^{-4}—while bold, italic, monospace and strikethrough each sit within ±0.003\pm 0.003 of zero. The same asymmetry appears in PDF. Colour is also the cue no mainstream converter preserves and no parsing benchmark scores, and it is common: 32.8%32.8\% of 6,4606{,}460 documents carry a deliberate colour or highlight, 10.3%10.3\% on an obligation. A pre-registered test shows that typing a cue for the agent adds +0.085+0.085 beyond merely preserving it (pHolm=0.049p_{\text{Holm}}=0.049). We validate the labels against rendered page images through an independent modality (κ=0.72\kappa=0.72) and bound what wording alone can achieve (AUC 0.6640.664). For agent builders the practical finding is that ingestion, not reasoning, is where this reliability is won or lost, and that the fix is cheap and measurable.

1 Introduction

An enterprise agent deployed in the wild does not read documents; it reads whatever an ingestion layer hands it. Before it can answer a compliance question, follow an operating procedure, or decide whether an action is permitted, some converter has turned a .docx or PDF into tokens. That layer is rarely the object of study, and it is where a large amount of an agent’s practical reliability is decided.

The failure we report is a property of that layer, and it has the shape that makes agent deployments hard to trust. It is not an outage and not an empty field. The pipeline reports success, the text looks complete, and the agent answers fluently and wrongly. Enterprise authors mark obligations visually—a red requirement, a highlighted exception, a struck-through value that no longer applies—and every mainstream converter we tested discards that layer while preserving the words around it. An agent reading the result sees a list of requirements with no indication which ones the author flagged, and, as we show, it guesses.

Three properties make this a safety-relevant ingestion problem rather than a formatting inconvenience. First, it is silent: nothing in the pipeline signals that information was dropped, so no monitor fires. Second, it inverts the usual failure mode: the agent does not abstain or return less, it asserts more, and its false-positive rate on requirements the author did not flag rises fourfold. Third, it is common, present in about a third of real documents, so it is not an adversarial edge case but the ordinary state of enterprise corpora.

The setting is demanding in ways that compound this. Enterprise procedural documents span 50–300 pages and mix formal definitions, step-by-step procedures, compliance rules, exception clauses, organisational charts, decision flowcharts, timelines and regulatory references—content whose semantics a human reader partly reconstructs from presentation rather than from wording. Documents are long enough that fixed-chunk ingestion fragments cross-references a reader resolves globally; content is heterogeneous, and several kinds of it (headers, footnotes, tracked revisions) are unreachable from a naive document walk; and authoring conventions are inconsistent, so the same visual device means different things across departments and must be interpreted rather than mapped one-to-one. Stated concretely, the problem is to produce a representation of such a document that a model can read without losing what the author encoded visually, and that is faithful, complete and economical enough to fit a context window.

This paper aims to contribute on three fronts. We quantify what formatting-blind ingestion costs an agent downstream, on real documents and against ground truth taken from the file’s own markup rather than from our judgement, and we show the effect holds across six answering models from two vendors. We localise it: a span-level leave-one-out over six cue classes attributes essentially the whole effect to colour and highlighting, with bold, italic, monospace and strikethrough contributing nothing measurable—which turns “formatting matters” into a specific, actionable claim about the two cues no mainstream converter preserves and no parsing benchmark scores. And we ask whether recovering a cue is enough, or whether an agent also needs to be told what the cue means; a pre-registered test says the latter, though the margin is modest and we report it as such. Alongside these we release a validated evaluation instrument: labels derived from OOXML run properties, scored deterministically with no LLM judge, checked against rendered page images through an independent modality, and bounded above by a supervised text-only classifier so that the task’s cue-dependence is measured rather than asserted. We also report what did not work, since both bear on how such systems should be built: progressive disclosure did not reduce token cost, and the typed layer shows no benefit on the two models that attempt the task only sparsely.

2 Related Work

Document conversion and benchmarks. A mature toolchain converts documents for agent consumption: python-docx and docx2python read OOXML directly, mammoth maps it to HTML, and Docling [4], Unstructured [16] and pymupdf4llm target LLM-ready Markdown. These are evaluated on text accuracy, reading order, tables and formulas—the axes of OmniDocBench [11] and ParseBench [12]—so character-level presentation sits largely outside that frame. Microsoft’s Office Comprehension Benchmark [10] is the first public suite evaluating LLM systems jointly on native Word, Excel and PowerPoint files, and we evaluate on its Word File-Fidelity track directly (§4.5); even there, formatting-dependent items are a minority and none turns on what a surviving cue means.

Formatting recognition. The closest refereed work is TexTAR [15], an ICDAR 2025 oral recognising textual attributes in document images. It covers precisely four—bold, italic, underline, strikeout—and neither colour nor highlighting, the two our ablation finds load-bearing. It also works from images and stops at attribute detection, where we recover cues from OOXML and PDF geometry, assign semantic roles, and measure the effect on answer correctness. Layout analysis [7, 18] models page geometry, which is complementary: our documents are text-heavy and their semantics sit in character properties.

Rendered versus ingested document. Liu et al. [9] mine the OOXML specification for 21 “evidence forks” under which a file presents one view in Office and another after extraction—plural ground truth. Every fork runs in the direction extraction reveals what the canvas hides, and their six dimensions contain no run-level character formatting; ours runs the other way. Yang et al. [5] establish the premise adversarially at USENIX Security: moderation systems “operate primarily on tokenized text and often overlook visual cues that humans naturally use”, a gap they exploit to reach over 86%86\% human recognition at under 1%1\% detection across 13 deployed systems. We differ from both in studying ordinary documents, where nobody crafted anything.

Is emphasis already a machine signal? Two findings bracket the question our ablation answers. PASTA [13] steers attention post hoc, motivated by exactly our premise—that writers “leverage the subtleties of text style, such as bold and italics, to guide the attention of readers”—reporting a 22%22\% average gain for LLAMA-7B. Against it, Dillitzer et al. [2] report an attention–performance divergence: emphasis redirects attention, yet “increased concentration does not inherently improve task accuracy”. Whether gains come from cue salience or cue typing is exactly what §4.4 pre-registers. Relatedly, Braun et al. [6] show prompt-side structure matters, but manipulate formatting the prompt author controls, not what the document author chose.

Typed extraction. Xu et al. [19] discover entity attributes without a predefined schema; we adopt their few-shot finding but replace mutual-dependency validation with source-quote verification, since a guided schema makes hallucination the risk that matters. Generic LLM extraction is competitive given suitable prompting [17]; REBEL [3] and ERNIE [20] extract triples for knowledge graphs, and work on legal contracts [8] shares the need for typed extraction but treats semantics as linguistically encoded. To our knowledge no prior system treats character-level formatting as a first-class extraction cue, and no benchmark scores whether a cue’s meaning reached the model.

3 Formatting-Aware Parsing

The parser reads the .docx file using python-docx and produces a flat list of RawBlock objects, each carrying structured formatting annotations. This stage is entirely code-based, with zero LLM calls.

3.1 Formatting as First-Class Signal

Parsing is the subject of this paper; the typed extraction and package rendering that consume its output are summarised in Appendix S5. The parser reads the .docx file with python-docx and emits a flat sequence of blocks carrying structured formatting annotations, entirely in code with zero LLM calls. Every contiguous run of text with identical formatting becomes a FormattingSpan, an immutable record of 12 attributes; eleven high-confidence formatting-to-semantics mappings then attach SemanticRole hints—red text or red highlight to critical_warning, any other visible highlight to warning, strikethrough to deprecated, and so on (Table 4, Appendix S4). These are hints, not ground truth: we deliberately exclude medium-confidence mappings such as green text to status marker, because a wrong hint biases an agent worse than no hint.

Blocks are serialized in a hybrid form. Markdown carries what a model has seen extensively in pretraining (**bold**, ˜˜struck˜˜); custom tags carry what Markdown cannot express ([COLOR:#FF0000], [HIGHLIGHT:YELLOW]); and structural tags carry document-level metadata a model cannot infer from text alone, such as which paragraphs belong to one ordered list. Appendix S4 enumerates the tag set.

3.2 Cue Disambiguation and Recovery

Cues are ambiguous and must be resolved before the text reaches an agent, and two of our rules were corrected during this study after corpus measurement contradicted the initial design. Bold means key_term when only some spans of a block carry it and implicit_heading when the block is a standalone line under 200 characters and entirely bold. Colour is matched by channel threshold rather than hex literal, which admits dark reds while excluding orange—though we note that 99.7%99.7\% of red spans in the corpus are exactly #FF0000, so the tolerance buys less than expected. Highlight is typed by presence, not hue: our initial rule typed only yellow, and measurement showed cyan and light-grey highlighting of obligations is common, so any highlight except WHITE/NONE—which render identically to unhighlighted text—now types as warning. That single correction raised the share of author-marked paragraphs receiving a salience role from 79.1%79.1\% to 97.6%97.6\%. Roles attach at block level while spans carry raw inline markers, and that separation is what makes the salience-versus-typing ablation possible.

Several kinds of content are unreachable from a w:body walk and were silently absent from our own representation until an external benchmark exposed it: headers and footers, footnotes, document properties, OMML equations, and—most consequentially—tracked changes, where a deletion is a w:r nested inside w:del carrying w:delText, so the accepted revision, the text actually in force, is discarded. Appendix S4 gives the full rule set and the OOXML paths.

4 Evaluation

Our claim is that a formatting cue carries meaning that survives or is destroyed during parsing, and that whether it survives changes whether a downstream model answers correctly. Testing this requires a task whose ground truth is the cue itself rather than our interpretation of it. We therefore evaluate on three levels: a real-document task at scale built from OOXML run properties (§4.1–4.4), an external benchmark whose questions we did not write (§4.5), and and a controlled test that the advantage survives an identical downstream pipeline (§S9).

All experiments use Claude Opus 4.6 unless stated, temperature 0. Question generation and second-opinion judging use different model families, so no model both writes and answers a question. Scripts, item sets, per-document content hashes and raw result JSON accompany the paper.

4.1 Corpus, prevalence, and task

We scanned 6,462 real .docx policy documents from a public corpus, named by content SHA-256, detecting cues at OOXML run level so nothing is inferred from wording. Walking the whole package, 32.8%32.8\% carry deliberate red text or a non-white highlight and 10.3%10.3\% carry one on a sentence expressing a modal obligation—the risk-bearing case; a further 2.6%2.6\% carry cues only outside the body, where no baseline we test can see them (Appendix S1).

This supports a real-document task at scale. A policy document contains several requirement-like sentences; the author marked some (red text or highlight) and left others unmarked. We ask:

List every requirement in this document that the author has singled out for special attention or elevated priority.

Ground truth is the marked set, taken directly from OOXML run properties—never from judgement. Scoring is set retrieval (precision, recall, F1) with a false-positive rate measured against real unmarked requirements from the same document, so a system that lists everything is penalised. Matching is lexical and deterministic: no LLM judge is involved. A gold requirement counts as retrieved when a run of four consecutive opening content words appears in the answer. That rule is deliberately conservative, and we verified it does not depress the numbers: only one of the 332 gold requirements has fewer than four content words and is therefore unmatchable by construction, giving every arm a recall ceiling of 0.9970.997, and no unmarked distractor is unmatchable at all. Relaxing the rule to a three-word run or 60% content-word overlap would accept a further 4.8%4.8\% of unmatched pairs, but inspection shows most of those are the looser rule wrongly matching a different requirement that shares boilerplate wording, so we keep the strict form. Construction requires at least one marked and at least three unmarked requirements per document, and rejects any document whose marked sentences are the only ones carrying urgency words. This yields 84 documents (332 marked, 4,192 unmarked distractors); 76–79 are scored in a given run, as a document is used only when every arm produces a representation under the size cap, so comparisons stay paired.

Is the task solvable without formatting? We measure this rather than assert it. Fitting a supervised text-only classifier (TF-IDF word 1–2 grams plus character 3–5 grams, logistic regression, grouped by document so no fold shares a document with its training split) to the marked/unmarked labels gives ROC AUC =0.664=0.664. The two interpretable heuristics a zero-shot reader could actually use sit at chance: an urgency-keyword rule scores 0.5080.508 and sentence length 0.4920.492. So the wording carries a weak signal recoverable only with supervision on the labels, and this 0.6640.664 is a ceiling on any formatting-blind method.

4.2 Formatting-blind conversion destroys answerability

Every arm receives the same question over the same document and differs only in how the document was parsed (Table 1).

Plain text scores 0.075 and docling 0.150, against 0.690 for our representation—a gap of +0.689+0.689 and +0.578+0.578 in per-document macro F1 (p<10−4p<10^{-4}, 62 of 76 and 57 of 76 documents won). These are not marginal effects. A formatting-blind converter sees the same sentences with no way to tell which the author marked, and the resulting answers are not merely incomplete: docling’s false-positive rate on genuinely unmarked requirements is 0.0430.043, roughly four times ours, because a system that cannot see the cue guesses.

The comparison that isolates preservation from pipeline depth is docx2python, which preserves character formatting as HTML and is the strongest baseline throughout. It reaches 0.5860.586—far above docling, far below ours, and the +0.110+0.110 gap to ours is significant even within this six-arm family (pHolm=0.022p_{\text{Holm}}=0.022).

4.3 The loss is concentrated in colour and highlight

“Formatting matters” is too coarse a claim to be useful. We localise it with a per-cue leave-one-out ablation: each arm removes exactly one cue class at the span level and re-derives the semantic roles, so document content is byte-identical across arms and only that cue’s markers and role token are absent (Figure 1).

The entire effect is carried by highlight (+0.302+0.302, pHolm<10−5p_{\text{Holm}}<10^{-5}) and colour (+0.262+0.262, pHolm=2×10−5p_{\text{Holm}}=2\times 10^{-5}). Bold, italic, monospace and strikethrough contribute nothing measurable—each within ±0.003\pm 0.003 of zero, with confidence intervals straddling it. This is not because those cues are absent: a single document carries over a thousand bold markers. It is because they are too common to be informative. An author who bolds every heading and defined term has not thereby singled anything out, whereas colouring or highlighting a requirement is a deliberate, sparing act. Cue typing pays only for cues rare enough to signal intent.

The ablation is also cue-specific, which validates that the manipulation does what it claims. Removing colour collapses colour-marked documents from 0.6990.699 to 0.2140.214 micro F1 while leaving highlight-marked documents at 0.6940.694; removing highlight does the mirror image, 0.659→0.1280.659\to 0.128, with colour-marked documents unchanged at 0.6700.670. Each removal therefore damages exactly the documents that use that cue and moves the others by at most 0.0110.011.

This localisation matters because colour is precisely the cue that mainstream conversion tools drop and that parsing benchmarks do not score. ParseBench’s formatting rules cover bold, italic, superscript and strikeout presence, with no rule type for font colour at all.

4.4 Does typing add anything beyond preserving?

The novel component of this system is not preserving cues—docx2python does that—but attaching typed roles to them. Isolating that contribution requires comparing our representation against the same representation with the role tokens removed and every inline cue marker retained.

This effect proved unstable across exploratory runs, for a reason we can name. Recovering headers, footers, footnotes and document properties (§4.5) raised the untyped arm from 0.5750.575 to 0.6100.610, shrinking the gap, and enlarging the arm family made the Holm correction stricter. Only 16 of 76 document pairs were discordant, so the test was underpowered either way. Rather than re-analyse the same data with different arm families, we pre-registered a confirmatory design— hypotheses, three arms, six repeats, test and correction family fixed in advance and committed to version control before execution.

We report that protocol’s execution history in full, because the borderline pp below depends on it. The design was executed once, then executed a second time, unchanged, after a defect in our parser was fixed: a table-cell renderer was emitting neutral colour markers ([COLOR:#000000] on ordinary black body text) which are spurious cues, so every ours representation changed and the earlier numbers could not stand. Nothing about the hypotheses, arms, repeats, test or correction family was altered. The pre-fix run gave +0.084+0.084 with W/L/T 15/2/6215/2/62 and pHolm=0.005p_{\text{Holm}}=0.005; the post-fix run, which is what we report, gives +0.085+0.085 with 13/4/6213/4/62 and pHolm=0.049p_{\text{Holm}}=0.049. The correction therefore made our headline pp worse while leaving the effect size unchanged, and the conclusion survives a change to the very parser it measures.

Both hypotheses are supported (Table 1, lower panel). Typing a preserved cue adds +0.085+0.085 macro F1 over showing the identical cue untyped (CI [+0.035,+0.145][+0.035,+0.145], pHolm=0.049p_{\text{Holm}}=0.049), and our representation beats the strongest preserving baseline by +0.107+0.107 (CI [+0.047,+0.174][+0.047,+0.174], pHolm=0.014p_{\text{Holm}}=0.014). Six repeats rather than three was decisive: averaging over more repeats removes per-call noise from each document’s score instead of parking it in the tie bucket, turning a 3/13 discordance against us into 13/4 in favour. H1 sits close to the threshold and we report it as such—the effect is consistent in sign and magnitude across every configuration we ran, but +0.085+0.085 should be read as an estimate with a wide interval rather than a precise quantity.

The typed arm here is the salience-filtered vocabulary—retaining only critical_warning, warning and deprecated—rather than the full role set, for a reason established in §4.6.

4.5 External validation: Microsoft OCB

The preceding task is ours, so we also evaluate on the File-Fidelity Word track of Microsoft’s Office Comprehension Benchmark [10]: 326 items over 59 documents across 14 features, with questions written by Microsoft and scored by OCB’s own weighted assertion satisfaction. Results are in Table 2.

We lead on the 38 formatting-dependent items (0.8160.816 against 0.7500.750) and on the 288 that are not about formatting (0.9770.977 against 0.8180.818), so the gain is not confined to the dimension this paper argues about. We are also the only system evaluated that answers document-property, comment and footnote questions at all.

Running the full track against our own system exposed two defects, both since fixed. We scored 0.000 on Header and Footer items where unstructured scored 1.0001.000, and every system including ours scored 0.0000.000 on Metadata and Footnote: none of headers, footers, footnotes, document properties or OMML equations is reachable from a w:body walk, so all five were silently absent. Adding them raised our overall score from 0.8530.853 to 0.9590.959. We also report where we lose: one Highlight item to docx2python, and a tie with docling on Equation.

4.6 Generalisation, and what does not replicate

A second format. The same asymmetry appears in PDF, which has no run properties, so cues must be recovered geometrically from character bounding boxes. Over all 126 born-digital formatting rules of ParseBench we match the strongest PDF baseline exactly on cue recovery (65/12665/126 each) while plain text extraction recovers none (0/1260/126) despite locating 107107 of 126126 targets. The only per-cue difference distinguishable in either direction is highlighting, where we lead 11/1811/18 against 4/184/18 (exact McNemar, p=0.039p=0.039). Table 5 in Appendix S8 gives the breakdown and the OCR caveat.

Six answering models. Repeating the task across two vendors and three capability tiers separates a robust finding from a fragile one (Figure 2; per-model statistics in Table 6). Cue preservation replicates overwhelmingly: plain text collapses under every model, from 0.0070.007 to 0.0750.075 micro F1. Beating docx2python replicates on four of six. Cue typing replicates on three of six, is positive on five, and is never significantly negative—but it is not universal, and we say so.

Where it fails. The two models showing no typing benefit are the two that barely attempt the task: Claude Sonnet 5 answers at recall 0.090.09 with precision 0.960.96. The same missing cue therefore produces opposite pathologies depending on the model—over-flagging in some, extreme abstention in others—and neither is detectable without ground truth.

The typed arm we report is the salience-filtered vocabulary, retaining only critical_warning, warning and deprecated. The full role set is dominated by structural tokens: across 40 documents implicit_heading occurs 2,136 times and emphasis 1,338, against 1,004 for critical_warning and 452 for warning. Roughly 62%62\% of role tokens therefore say nothing about whether the author singled a passage out, and a model that treats any role token as a flag over-triggers—which is what we observed on a weaker model excluded by the competence screen below. Restricting the vocabulary fixes it, and under Claude the filtered and full sets are statistically indistinguishable (p=0.45p=0.45).

Model eligibility was decided by a criterion, not by inspection. Typed hints require a model to use a hint discriminatively, which is an instruction-following capability, so a model that cannot do the task at all cannot be interpreted on formatting cues. Each candidate therefore answered the same question over a formatting-free control document in which the flagged requirements are named explicitly in prose, with thresholds fixed in advance (macro F1 ≥0.80\geq 0.80, false-positive rate ≤0.05\leq 0.05). All six reported models pass (macro F1 0.8740.874–0.9760.976, FP rate 0.0030.003–0.0370.037). One further model, Mistral Large 3, fails both at 0.5580.558 and 0.1330.133: its control precision is 0.4800.480, meaning it flags about as many unmarked requirements as marked ones when the answer is written out in words. Over-flagging is a baseline property of that model rather than a response to our hints, so it is out of population; we report its numbers in Appendix S10 rather than discarding them.

4.7 Does the advantage survive an identical downstream pipeline?

Handing a parsed representation straight to the answering model invites the objection that we compared a full pipeline against bare converters. Running the complete pipeline per arm over 68 documents—an identical extraction prompt, model and tier logic, identical image bytes, identical renderer, varying only the parsed text—the advantage survives and grows (Table 3).

The interpretive key is that all three arms retain a similar share of the gold requirement text in the final package (0.6650.665, 0.6340.634, 0.6070.607), so the gap is not content loss: only our package still records which requirements the author singled out. Table 3 gives the numbers.

4.8 Implications for agents deployed in the wild

Three consequences follow for anyone running document-consuming agents in production.

The failure is invisible to standard monitoring. Every arm we tested returns well-formed output on every document; none raises, none reports missing content. A pipeline health check, a schema validator, and a token-count sanity check all pass. The only signal is answer quality on questions whose ground truth lives in the source markup—which is precisely what an operator does not have. This argues for ingestion-level assertions rather than output-level monitoring: our own parser now asserts that a recovered cue implies a located span, and that assertion caught a defect we had already published in a table.

It degrades precision, not just recall, which is the wrong direction for autonomy. An agent that returns less is inconvenient; an agent that confidently returns more is dangerous, because a downstream action may be taken on a requirement the author never flagged. docling’s false-positive rate on unmarked requirements is 0.0430.043 against our 0.0110.011. Under two of the six answering models the effect appears as extreme conservatism instead—recall 0.090.09 at precision 0.960.96—so the same missing signal produces opposite pathologies depending on the model, and neither is detectable without ground truth.

The fix is cheap, and it belongs before the agent. Recovering these cues is deterministic, code-only, and costs no LLM calls; the entire effect reported here comes from parsing alone. It does cost tokens—roughly twice plain text—so it is a deliberate trade of context budget for factuality rather than a free win. Notably, the cue must be typed and not merely passed through: showing an agent [COLOR:#FF0000] is worth less than telling it the span is a critical warning (+0.085+0.085, pHolm=0.049p_{\text{Holm}}=0.049), which is consistent with evidence that emphasis redirects model attention without accuracy reliably following [2].

5 Conclusion

An enterprise agent reads whatever its ingestion layer produces, and that layer silently discards the meaning authors encode visually. On 76 real policy documents, recovering the requirements an author singled out falls from micro F1 0.6900.690 to 0.1500.150 (docling) and 0.0750.075 (plain text), a gap that replicates across six answering models from two vendors. The failure is the difficult kind for autonomy: not an error the pipeline reports, but an agent that answers fluently and wrongly, with four times the false-positive rate on requirements the author never flagged.

The loss is localised. A per-cue leave-one-out attributes essentially all of it to highlight (+0.302+0.302) and colour (+0.262+0.262), both pHolm<10−4p_{\text{Holm}}<10^{-4}, with bold, italic, monospace and strikethrough each within ±0.003\pm 0.003 of zero—and the same asymmetry reappears in PDF. Colour is simultaneously the cue that matters most and the one no mainstream converter preserves and no parsing benchmark scores. A pre-registered test further shows that typing a cue for the agent adds +0.085+0.085 beyond preserving it (pHolm=0.049p_{\text{Holm}}=0.049), consistent with evidence that emphasis redirects attention without accuracy reliably following [2].

Limitations. Exposure is common but not universal: a third of documents carry a deliberate colour or highlight and 10.3%10.3\% carry one on an obligation. PDF support requires a usable text layer, since we do not OCR. The typed layer is robust on three of the six models but shows no benefit on two that attempt the task only sparsely, so it is conditional on the model engaging with the hint. Ground truth is derived automatically from run properties and validated against rendered pages by an independent modality (κ=0.72\kappa=0.72) but not yet by human annotators, which is the most valuable addition remaining. The task is unsaturated at recall 0.600.60, and this is genuine difficulty rather than measurement: the scorer’s structural ceiling is 0.9970.997. Our representation costs roughly twice plain text in tokens, a deliberate trade of context budget for factuality. Absolute micro F1 is stable only to about ±0.08\pm 0.08 across configurations, so every claim rests on paired per-document tests.

Future work. Human validation of the labels; OCR-backed cue recovery for scanned pages; non-English documents, where these cues carry culturally inflected semantics; and diff-based re-ingestion across revisions, for which tracked changes already supply reviewer-signed ground truth.

Appendix S1 Corpus and Prevalence

We scanned 6,462 real .docx files from a public corpus of policy and procedural documents (files are named by content SHA-256, so provenance is verifiable and de-duplication is exact). Scanning is done at OOXML run level, so nothing is inferred from wording. Appendix 7 gives the full breakdown by pattern: a colour or highlight marking on a constraint occurs in 359 documents, manual strikethrough in 35, and Word tracked changes in 40. Tracked changes were invisible to our earlier scans, because a tracked deletion is a w:r nested inside w:del carrying w:delText, which neither paragraph.runs nor iter_inner_content reaches.

Two figures matter here and they differ by a factor of three, so we give both. Walking the entire OOXML package, 32.8% of documents carry deliberate red text or a non-white highlight somewhere, and 10.3% carry one on a sentence expressing a modal obligation—the risk-bearing case, since that is where a dropped cue changes what a reader is told to do. The stricter pattern C above (5.6%) requires the marked run rather than the marked sentence to carry the obligation, and therefore undercounts by roughly 1.8×1.8\times; we report it because it is the population the task in §4.1 is built from, not because it is the prevalence of the phenomenon. A further 2.6% of documents carry cues only outside the body—in headers, footers, footnotes or comments—which no baseline we test can see at all.

Appendix S3 Tracked Changes

Tracked changes. Word revisions give the strongest ground truth available—the reviewer’s own recorded edit. Across 28 recorded revisions ours carries both the superseded and in-force value with the superseded one marked in 27 cases, while no other arm marks it even once; plain text loses the value entirely in 16 and surfaces only the superseded value in 3, an outright factual error. On forced-choice accuracy we and docx2python are indistinguishable (0.8180.818 versus 0.8330.833 at n≈35n\!\approx\!35), because a converter that silently discards w:del is accidentally right. At n=12n=12 items this cannot carry a claim and we do not rest one on it.

Appendix S4 Stage-1 Rules in Full

S4.1 Formatting Disambiguation

The raw mapping in Table 4 conceals ambiguity that must be resolved before the text reaches a model. The rules below are the ones the released parser applies; two of them were corrected during this study after corpus measurement contradicted our initial design, and we give both the rule and the correction because the corrections are themselves findings.

Inline versus standalone bold. Bold triggers key_term or implicit_heading depending on context, and the discriminator is not a coverage ratio. A block is standalone when its plain text is a single line shorter than 200 characters. A standalone block whose every span is bold—or whose text is entirely upper case—becomes implicit_heading; otherwise a block with some but not all spans bold becomes key_term. One consequence is worth stating because it is a genuine gap rather than a design choice: an all-bold paragraph of 200 characters or more matches neither branch and receives no bold-derived role at all (29 such blocks in a 29,170-block sweep). We considered a character-coverage ratio instead and found it no better on the threshold sweep, so the simpler standalone test ships.

Colour as fuzzy matching. Authors do not use canonical RGB values: a red warning may be #FF0000, #C00000, #CC0000 or a custom hue chosen years ago. Rather than matching hex literals the parser thresholds the channels, is_red(r,g,b)=(r>180)∧(g<80)∧(b<80)(r,g,b)=(r>180)\wedge(g<80)\wedge(b<80), which admits dark reds while excluding orange and maroon. We report one honest deflation of this design: on the real corpus 99.7%99.7\% of red spans are exactly #FF0000, so the tolerance costs nothing but buys much less than we expected.

Highlight is typed by presence, not by hue. Our initial rule typed only yellow and dark-yellow highlights as warning. Corpus measurement showed this was wrong: cyan and light-grey highlighting of obligations is common, and those spans reached the model carrying their raw value with no role attached. The shipped rule therefore types any highlight as warning except WHITE and NONE, which render identically to unhighlighted text and are not marks at all; a RED highlight escalates to critical_warning alongside red text. Hue is still preserved in the serialized output, so a reader that wants to distinguish yellow from cyan can. This change raised the share of author-marked paragraphs receiving a salience role from 79.1%79.1\% to 97.6%97.6\%, and it is the single correction with the largest effect on our results.

Roles are attached at block level. A role is computed from the properties of a block’s spans but recorded on the block, serialized as a tag attribute (roles="CRITICAL_WARNING"). Individual spans carry their raw cue markers inline ([COLOR:#FF0000], [HIGHLIGHT:YELLOW], ~~struck~~) but not role names. This distinction is what makes the ablation in §4.4 possible: removing the roles attribute leaves every inline marker intact, so cue salience and cue typing can be varied independently over byte-identical content.

S4.2 Hybrid Serialization Protocol

After parsing, blocks are serialized to an annotated text string for LLM consumption. The serialization design involves three interlocking choices:

Hybrid Markdown + custom tags. Standard Markdown handles formatting the LLM has seen extensively in pretraining: bold (**text**), italic (*text*), and strikethrough (˜˜text˜˜). For formatting with no Markdown equivalent, we use custom tags: [COLOR:red]...[/COLOR], [HIGHLIGHT:yellow]...[/HIGHLIGHT]. This hybrid is 15–20% more token-efficient than pure custom-tag serialization while exploiting the model’s Markdown familiarity.

Structural metadata tags. Every block is wrapped in a structural tag (e.g. [HEADING level=2 style="Heading 2"], [TABLE has_header=True cols=4]) carrying document-level metadata that the LLM cannot infer from text alone: which numbered paragraphs are part of an ordered list, which table has a header row, which paragraph sits under a given heading level. Without these, the extraction model would need to re-derive heading hierarchy from font size heuristics, a fragile and error-prone operation. Tag attributes additionally carry fine-grained context—indentation depth, font size, and Word style name. Appendix S14 enumerates the full tag set and attribute encoding.

Appendix S13 details the complete formatting-to-LLM pipeline for all 11 active SemanticRoles: the raw Word attribute, the disambiguation rule applied at parse time, the resulting role, the exact serialization the LLM receives, and the extraction signal that role encodes. Appendix S15 walks a worked parsing example end to end, and Appendix S16 documents the XML-level workarounds required for content python-docx does not natively expose (text boxes, tracked changes, comments, merged cells, OLE objects).

S4.3 Content Unreachable from a Body Walk

A .docx is an OPC package, not a single stream, and several kinds of content sit outside the part that a naive walk traverses. Each of the following was silently absent from our own representation until an external benchmark exposed it (§4.5), and each remains absent from most converters we test:

  • •

    Headers and footers live in separate parts, up to three per section (default, first page, even page). They carry document-control facts—version, effective date, classification marking—and a red draft or highlighted classification in a header is precisely the signal this work concerns, so we parse them with character formatting intact and label which is primary.

  • •

    Footnotes, endnotes and document properties occupy their own parts; Word’s separator notes must be skipped.

  • •

    Tracked changes. A tracked deletion is a w:r nested inside w:del carrying w:delText rather than w:t, and an insertion nests inside w:ins. Neither is a direct child of the paragraph, so both are invisible to a run-level walk—which means the accepted revision, the text actually in force, is discarded. We walk the paragraph’s children in document order and map the semantics onto the existing vocabulary: an insertion is current text, a deletion is content the author retired, which is what strikethrough already means here.

  • •

    Equations, hyperlinks and text boxes, whose characters sit in m:t inside m:oMath or in runs nested rather than direct.

Two robustness points follow from running at corpus scale. Real documents violate the specification—one declares a fractional half-point font size, which makes a strict reader raise and abandon the whole file—so a malformed cue must degrade to “cue absent”, never to “document unreadable”. And python-docx reconstructs each table row from the table grid, raising when a vertical merge references a row that supplies no cell at that offset; we fall back to reading the row’s cells directly from the XML, which loses merge continuation but preserves the text. Both defects aborted a 6,462-document scan on first contact.

For born-digital PDF the same cues must be recovered geometrically, since PDF has no run properties: a highlight is a filled rectangle drawn behind glyphs, and a strikethrough is a hairline crossing the glyph midline where an underline sits at the baseline. We therefore classify from character-level bounding boxes rather than span-level ones—a span-level comparison fails because the renderer merges struck and live text into a single span (§S8).

Appendix S5 System Architecture and Tiering

The system processes documents in three stages (diagrammed in Figure 3, Appendix S12). Stage 1 (Parse & Serialize) is entirely code-based with zero LLM calls, and is the subject of this paper: it recovers character-level presentation and emits annotated text. Stage 2 (Extract) and Stage 3 (Render) consume that text and are described in §S7. The separation concentrates LLM reasoning where it adds value— entity classification, relationship identification, editorial summarization—and keeps deterministic work in code. Five design principles guide the architecture (Appendix S12), the most consequential being formatting is signal, not decoration and source-quote provenance.

Appendix S6 Adaptive Tiering by Document Size

Because Stage 2’s cost is what makes a formatting-faithful representation practical at enterprise document sizes, we note the tiering here and specify it in Appendix S22. A tier is selected from the annotated document’s estimated token count: a single extraction call below 25K tokens (most enterprise SOPs), the same plus faithfulness validation on a 20% sample to 50K, and above that segmentation into up to 16 overlapping ∼\sim8K-token chunks merged pairwise, costing 2​N−12N{-}1 calls for NN segments — 3 at N=2N{=}2, rising to 31 at the maximum. Segments are kept small deliberately so each call completes inside the service’s ∼\sim330 s streaming limit; wall-clock time is 30 seconds to 8 minutes depending on tier.

A uniform 4K-token chunking alternative would need an estimated 40–80 calls for a 100-page document and would fragment extractions across chunk boundaries; that figure is analytical, from the chunk count, and not a measured baseline. The tiered design instead exploits the fact that one long-context call yields globally coherent output, able to deduplicate and resolve cross-references in a single pass.

Appendix S7 From Representation to Agent-Loadable Knowledge

A faithful representation is a means, not an end. Our reference implementation carries it through two further stages so an agent can load the result directly: one LLM call per document (or per segment) converts the annotated text into 17 typed entity types joined by 14 relationships under a mandate that every entity carry a verbatim source_quote, and a content-analysis router then writes those entities into a five-file progressive-disclosure package in which the entry point holds operative guardrails and reference material moves to sub-files (Appendices S13–S25). Document size is handled by tiering (§S6); embedded diagrams add one vision call per non-decorative image.

What matters for an agent is that the cue survives the whole pipeline. Measured over 34 generated packages, a colour- or highlight-marked requirement reaches the quick-reference file at rate 0.5690.569 against 0.2450.245 for an unmarked one—a 2.3×2.3\times enrichment—so an agent that loads only the entry point and the cheat sheet still encounters disproportionately what the author flagged. §S9 tests whether the Stage-1 advantage survives this pipeline; generalising it to a measured claim about typed-extraction accuracy would need a benchmark that does not yet exist, and is future work.

Appendix S8 Cross-Format Results: PDF

If colour is the load-bearing cue, that should hold in a format encoded entirely differently. PDF has no run properties: a highlight is a filled rectangle drawn behind glyphs and a strikethrough is a hairline crossing the glyph midline, so cues must be recovered geometrically from character bounding boxes. We evaluate on all 126 born-digital formatting rules of ParseBench (Table 5).

Two things follow. First, plain PDF text extraction recovers no cue at all (0/1260/126) while locating 107107 of the 126126 targets—the same pattern as in Word, where the information is present on the page and absent from the tokens. Second, we match the strongest PDF baseline exactly on cue recovery (65/12665/126 each, 9 discordant rules in each direction), and the only statistically distinguishable per-cue difference in either direction is highlighting, where we lead 11/1811/18 against 4/184/18 (p=0.039p=0.039); bold is identical, and our lower italic and strikethrough counts are not significant (p=0.125p=0.125, p=0.500p=0.500). The cross-format picture therefore reproduces the Word result—broad parity, with the colour-class cue as the differentiator—from a different encoding and scored by a benchmark we did not write.

Two limitations. Our text localisation trails pymupdf4llm (7575 versus 8282 of 126126), so part of the italic and strikethrough shortfall is a reading-order deficit rather than cue detection, and improving reading order would likely close it. And 18 of the 126 rules name text that is absent from the PDF’s native text layer entirely: there, every arm recovers zero cues, and pymupdf4llm locates text on 4 of them only by silently invoking OCR. We report those rules rather than excluding them, since excluding them would change no cue number. Cue recovery for scanned pages, where the cue survives as pixels but no text layer exists, needs OCR we do not perform and is left to future work.

Appendix S9 Equal-Preprocessing Comparison

Every experiment so far hands a parsed representation straight to the answering model, which invites the objection that we compared a full pipeline against bare converters. We therefore ran the complete pipeline—an identical extraction prompt, model and tier logic, identical image bytes for the vision pass, identical renderer—over 68 documents, varying only the Stage-1 text, and asked the same question of the rendered knowledge package (Table 3).

The advantage survives, and grows: +0.178+0.178 over docx2python (27/5/36, CI [+0.080,+0.277][+0.080,+0.277]) and +0.422+0.422 over docling (40/2/26), both significant. So the effect is attributable to the representation rather than to pipeline depth.

The retention column explains why, and is the more informative result. All three arms carry a similar share of the gold requirement text through extraction and rendering into the final package—0.6650.665, 0.6340.634, 0.6070.607—so the gap is not a matter of content being lost. It is that only our package still records which of those requirements the author singled out. Salience survives the pipeline as placement: a marked requirement reaches the quick-reference file at rate 0.5690.569 against 0.2450.245 for an unmarked one, a 2.3×2.3\times enrichment.

Absolute scores are lower than in §4.2 for every arm, because extraction and rendering deliberately compress and restructure, and because a 0.6650.665 retention rate caps recall. We report the comparison rather than the absolute level. On faithfulness, a validator sample of 24 entities on a held-out enterprise SOP found every entity traceable to a verbatim source quote at f⁡(e)≥2f(e)\!\geq\!2 (87.5%87.5\% fully faithful, the remainder under-specifying rather than fabricating); Appendix S31 traces a complete run stage by stage.

Appendix S12 Architectural Design Principles

Five principles guide the system’s architecture:

  1. 1.

    LLM for reasoning, code for assembly. LLM calls handle tasks requiring judgment (entity classification, relationship inference, editorial summarization). Deterministic tasks (parsing, serialization, rendering, file I/O) remain in code. This minimizes cost, maximizes reproducibility, and reduces non-determinism.

  2. 2.

    Formatting is signal, not decoration. Every formatting attribute (bold, italic, color, highlight, font) is preserved through the pipeline and presented to the LLM as a semantic hint. The pipeline never strips formatting.

  3. 3.

    Source-quote provenance. Every extracted entity must cite a verbatim quote from the source document. This is the primary anti-hallucination mechanism, more effective than any post-hoc validation.

  4. 4.

    Type specificity over generality. Seventeen entity types with distinct schemas produce richer extractions than a generic “extract all entities” approach. A Procedure has steps with actors and deadlines; a Rule has conditions and consequences. These distinctions matter for downstream use.

  5. 5.

    Progressive disclosure over monolithic output. The output is not a single flat document but a tiered package: a lean entry point containing critical guardrails, a quick-reference sheet for common lookups, and typed sub-files loaded on demand. This matches how AI assistants actually consume skill content.

Appendix S13 Complete Formatting-to-LLM Pipeline

Table 8 details the complete formatting-to-LLM pipeline for all 11 active SemanticRoles introduced in Table 4.

Appendix S14 Serialization Tag Set and Attribute Encoding

Structural metadata tags. Every block is wrapped in a structural tag carrying document-level metadata:

  • •

    [HEADING level=2 style="Heading 2"] — heading level and Word style name

  • •

    [TABLE has_header=True cols=4] — table structure hints

  • •

    [IMAGE type="flowchart" size=45K] — image classification placeholder

  • •

    [PARAGRAPH roles="CRITICAL_WARNING"] — block-level roles

These structural tags encode information the LLM cannot infer from text alone: which numbered paragraphs are part of an ordered list, which table has a header row, which paragraph sits under a given heading level. Without these, the extraction model would need to re-derive heading hierarchy from font size heuristics, a fragile and error-prone operation.

Attribute encoding for fine-grained context. Tag attributes also carry indentation depth (for nested lists), font size (to distinguish normal body text from large callout headings), and style name (which encodes the Word template’s intended semantic, e.g., “Caption”, “List Number 2”). Style names are particularly valuable because they reflect the document author’s own semantic intent, which often aligns with entity type triggers.

Appendix S16 Handling python-docx Limitations

Several content types common in enterprise documents are not natively exposed by python-docx and require XML-level access:

  • •

    Text boxes: Content in w:txbxContent elements must be extracted by walking the XML tree directly.

  • •

    Tracked changes: python-docx silently skips deleted text. Insertions (w:ins) and deletions (w:del) require XML parsing.

  • •

    Comments: Stored in word/comments.xml, accessible only through the OPC package interface.

  • •

    Merged cells: Vertical merge continuations (tc.vMerge) report as empty cells.

  • •

    OLE objects: Embedded objects appear as empty paragraphs; detected via w:object elements and logged as warnings.

These workarounds add approximately 80 lines of XML-handling code but are essential for complete extraction from real-world enterprise documents.

Appendix S17 Why 17 Entity Types?

Fewer types (e.g., the 6-type schema common in generic IE) force-fit distinct content into overly broad categories: a Rule with conditions and consequences is fundamentally different from a Procedure with ordered steps, even though both describe “what to do.” The 17-type taxonomy was validated against real enterprise SOPs to ensure each type has clear, non-overlapping trigger signals.

Appendix S18 The 12-Point Extraction Mandate

Beyond the obvious “extract all entities” instruction, several rules address specific failure modes observed in early testing:

  • •

    Read-before-extract: The model must read the entire document before beginning extraction, preventing the common failure mode where entities in later sections are missed because the model starts outputting before fully reading.

  • •

    Checklist-as-procedure: Checkbox lists are Procedure entities, not Warning entities, even if they contain prohibitions. Without this rule, models frequently misclassify “checklist items to verify” as warnings.

  • •

    WRONG/CORRECT pattern: When a document presents “Incorrect: X / Correct: Y” examples, these become worked_examples in the type_specific_fields of a Rule entity. Without this rule, the WRONG examples are sometimes extracted as independent factual claims.

  • •

    Procedural completeness: Sub-steps within a step must be preserved in full. The model must never “summarize” a 12-step sub-procedure into a one-line description. This rule prevents the single most common form of information loss in SOP extraction.

  • •

    Warnings and prohibitions are highest priority: Even if the surrounding content is low-confidence, a Warning entity with red text and explicit consequences must always be extracted at HIGH confidence.

The remaining 7 points of the 12-point mandate cover standard but necessary rules: ALL-CAPS lines as implicit headings, proper Enumeration item extraction (preserve all items verbatim), Scope entity completeness, Metric unit and threshold preservation, cross-reference tracking for relationship extraction, confidence calibration for diagram-derived entities, and deduplication precedence (explicit stated entity wins over diagram-inferred).

Appendix S19 Few-Shot Example Selection

The five few-shot examples included in the extraction prompt, each targeting a specific failure mode:

  1. 1.

    A Definition with bold formatting (demonstrates key term detection from inline bold).

  2. 2.

    A Procedure from a numbered list (demonstrates step extraction with actors and deadlines).

  3. 3.

    A complex paragraph yielding Rule + Exception + Form_or_Template simultaneously (multi-entity extraction from a single passage—the most common source of extraction errors).

  4. 4.

    A Procedure with nested sub-steps and an embedded Warning (demonstrates that sub-steps must be preserved in full and warnings extracted as siblings, not merged into the procedure).

  5. 5.

    A Rule with WRONG/CORRECT worked examples (demonstrates that comparison tables encode the rule’s worked_examples field, not separate factual entities).

Appendix S21 Structured Output via Tool Use

Free-form type_specific_fields. The tool use schema intentionally leaves type_specific_fields as a free-form JSON object rather than defining a per-type nested schema. This avoids an excessively deep and brittle tool definition (>>200 lines of JSON Schema) while still guiding the model through the system prompt’s per-type field descriptions. The Pydantic model that receives the output validates only the required fields, tolerating per-type variation.

The system uses the Strands Agents SDK with a @strands.tool-decorated function as the extraction target. The model is forced to call extract_entities with the full ExtractionResult payload, which Pydantic validates before returning to the pipeline. This guarantees valid structured output without JSON parsing heuristics. The agent’s message history is inspected post-call to extract the tool input dict, which is then deserialized into typed Python models.

Appendix S22 Tier 3 Merge: Additional Details

Segmentation walk. The algorithm walks blocks sequentially, accumulating a running token count and starting a new segment when the 8,000-token threshold is exceeded.

Oversized block handling during segmentation. A subtle complication arises with oversized blocks—single paragraphs exceeding 2×2\times the overlap budget (i.e., >>8,000 characters). Including these in the overlap would cause them to dominate the next segment’s context, crowding out the actual boundary content. Such blocks are explicitly excluded from overlap computation via a skip_next_overlap flag, ensuring the overlap consists of the intended preceding context rather than one large anomalous block.

Restore from originals. After merging, the compact summaries are replaced with full original data by matching merged entity names to original segment entities via case-insensitive string matching. For entities that appeared in multiple segments (cross-segment duplicates), the merge call identifies them as a single entity; the restore step takes the union of all source_quotes arrays and merges type_specific_fields (e.g., unioning steps arrays from both segments ensures no sub-steps are lost during deduplication).

Appendix S23 Why Source-Quote Verification Instead of Mutual Dependency?

The ZOES Mutual Dependency (MD) principle validates (entity, attribute, value) triplets by checking if masking one component allows recovery of the others. MD addresses attribute granularity—ensuring discovered attributes are neither too coarse nor too fine. In our guided-schema extraction, attributes are predefined, so the granularity problem MD solves does not exist. The actual risk is hallucination: the LLM fabricating content not in the source. Source-quote verification targets this risk directly with a simpler prompt and lower cost.

Appendix S25 Progressive Disclosure: Package Layout and File Roles

SKILL.md (entry point). Contains the YAML frontmatter, a “How to Use This Skill” section linking to sub-files, and only the action-critical content: scope, prerequisites, exceptions, bare guardrail rules, warnings, and short procedures/enumerations. Strict size target: <<500 lines. Entities routed to sub-files appear as one-line stubs with a “See docs/X.md” link.

QUICK_REFERENCE.md (auto-generated cheat sheet). Auto-generated from all Warning entities and high-severity Rule entities. Contains severity annotations, consequence statements, and mitigation guidance. Only generated when such entities exist. This file is the first reference an AI assistant should consult—it surfaces the most operationally critical constraints without requiring navigation into deeper sub-files.

docs/ sub-files (full reference content). Each sub-file uses the same hierarchy-aware rendering as SKILL.md but with full entity content: complete procedure steps with actor annotations, full enumeration tables with attribute columns, metric formulas and targets, glossary terms and definitions. Sub-files are loaded on demand, keeping the main context window lean.

references/provenance.json. Maps every entity ID to its source quotes, source section path, and extraction confidence. Enables complete auditability: any AI-generated statement derived from the skill can be traced to a verbatim source passage.

Appendix S26 Anthropic-Spec Description Generation

The SKILL.md YAML frontmatter requires a description field that the Anthropic skill specification calls “pushy”—it must use imperative trigger language to combat undertriggering (the failure mode where the AI assistant possesses the skill but fails to load it because the user’s query doesn’t explicitly mention the skill name).

The description generation algorithm uses a three-tier fallback:

  1. 1.

    Audience + entity trigger keywords (primary): Extract applies_to from the Scope entity as audience context. Collect up to 5 Procedure, Rule, and Warning entity names as trigger keywords. Format: ‘‘For {audience}. Use this skill whenever users ask about {entity_names}.’’11 1 Entity names from the document are preferred over applies_to as triggers because they match the vocabulary users employ when asking questions (“How do I reset a password?”) rather than the document’s audience description (“IT Support team handling end-user requests”).

  2. 2.

    SCOPE entity summary (fallback): If no Scope entity has applies_to, use the scope entity’s LLM-generated summary as the description.

  3. 3.

    Domain + high-confidence entity names (last resort): Use the document title plus names of HIGH-confidence Definition, Rule, and Procedure entities.

Appendix S27 Running Example: Rendered Output

The extracted entities from our onboarding SOP produce the following SKILL.md structure:

Note the key rendering decisions: (a) name and description are the only frontmatter fields (Anthropic spec); (b) entity headers carry no type labels (removed as presentation noise); (c) the long Procedure appears as a one-line stub with a sub-file link; (d) the Warning is rendered as a blockquote with CRITICAL severity inline in SKILL.md.

Appendix S28 Open-Schema Discovery

The 17-type taxonomy covers approximately 95% of enterprise SOP content. For novel document types containing structures outside the taxonomy (e.g., escalation matrices, audit checklists), the system supports an optional open-schema discovery mode inspired by ZOES’s Root Attribute Induction [19].

The approach uses a two-pass prompt strategy: Pass 1 adds the instruction “if you encounter structured information that does not fit any of the 17 types, create a new type with a descriptive name and define its schema” to the standard extraction prompt. If novel types are discovered, Pass 2 re-extracts with the expanded taxonomy to ensure consistent application across the entire document.

Appendix S29 Conflict Resolution

When the source document contains contradictory information (e.g., “probationary period is 90 days” in Section 1 vs. “60 days for part-time employees” in Section 7), the system: (1) flags the entity with a conflict marker, (2) preserves both values with source citations, (3) adds an entry to a dedicated “Conflicts & Ambiguities” section in the output, and (4) lowers the entity’s confidence. The system never silently resolves contradictions—that decision belongs to a human reviewer.

Appendix S30 Implementation Details

Architecture and dependencies. The system is implemented as a Python 3.12+ package comprising ∼\sim1,800 lines of production code across 10 modules. The largest modules are: llm/prompts.py (∼\sim763 lines, extraction + merge + validation prompts), rendering/skill_renderer.py (∼\sim1,100 lines, entity routing and multi-file rendering), and llm/extraction.py (∼\sim630 lines, tier orchestration, segmentation, and binary merge).

The five runtime dependencies are: python-docx (≥\geq0.8.11) for document parsing, an agent SDK (≥\geq0.1.0) for LLM calls against a managed cloud LLM service, pydantic (≥\geq2.0) for structured output validation, click (≥\geq8.0) for CLI, and rich (≥\geq13.0) for progress display. Notably absent: NumPy, sentence-transformers, FAISS, scikit-learn—the embedding-based deduplication machinery common in document processing pipelines is entirely replaced by inline LLM deduplication.

Bedrock integration. LLM calls use the Strands Agents SDK’s BedrockModel with cross-region inference profiles (us.anthropic.claude-opus-4-6-v1 for all calls: extraction, merge, faithfulness verification, and vision). The SDK handles streaming, retry with exponential backoff (delay=2attempt+jitter\text{delay}=2^{\text{attempt}}+\text{jitter}), and structured output via tool use.

Errors are classified as retryable (throttling, rate limits, transient server errors, connection timeouts) or non-retryable (authentication failures, expired tokens, malformed requests, maximum token exceeded). On retry exhaustion after 3 attempts, a PipelineError is raised with context about the failed tier and call index, enabling targeted debugging.

Appendix S31 End-to-End Example

This appendix traces the complete pipeline execution on the included test document, test_doc.docx—an IT Password Reset Procedure SOP. All inputs and outputs shown are real data from an actual pipeline run.

S31.1 Stage 1 Input: Source Document Structure

The input is a Word document with 8 sections: Scope, Prerequisites, Password Reset Steps, Security Warning, Account Lockout Policy, Compliance Logging Rule, Service Level Targets, and Glossary. The document exercises three key formatting signals:

  • •

    Bold runs: “password reset process”, step labels (“Log in:”, “Locate account:”, etc.), policy terms (“Lockout threshold:”, “1 hour”).

  • •

    Red text (RGB 255, 0, 0): The entire Security Warning paragraph triggers Critical_Warning role.

  • •

    Heading styles: Heading 1/2 triggers heading hierarchy reconstruction.

S31.2 Stage 1 Output: Hybrid Serialization (excerpt)

The parser serializes the warning paragraph with its semantic role tag:

⬇
[HEADING level=2]Security Warning[/HEADING]
[COLOR:red][CRITICAL_WARNING]NEVER share temporary passwords via email
or chat messages. Email is not a secure channel and violates the
company security policy. Always use a phone call or an encrypted
messaging platform.[/CRITICAL_WARNING][/COLOR]

Bold key terms in the lockout section are annotated inline:

⬇
[HEADING level=1]Account Lockout Policy[/HEADING]
**Lockout threshold:** Accounts are automatically locked after
**5 consecutive failed login attempts**.
**Lockout duration:** 30 minutes. IT admins may unlock accounts
manually before the window expires.

S31.4 Stage 3 Output: Progressive Disclosure Package

The content-analysis router distributes all 20 entities across 5 output files:

  • •

    SKILL.md (113 lines): Scope, all 3 prerequisites, 4 rules (bare constraints), 1 warning, 1 exception. The Procedure entity (6 steps) is routed to docs/ and replaced with a stub link.

  • •

    QUICK_REFERENCE.md: Auto-generated from the 1 Warning entity + 4 critical Rule entities, formatted for instant lookup.

  • •

    docs/procedures-reference.md: Full 6-step password reset procedure with actor, prerequisites, and postconditions.

  • •

    docs/concepts-and-metrics.md: 1 Definition, 3 Metric entities (resolution time, SLA, audit cycle), 3 Glossary_Entry entities.

  • •

    references/provenance.json: Full source-quote map for all 20 entities.
